notes:
1. Meaning of State Legislature

  • The State Legislature is the law-making body of the State Government.
  • It represents the people of the State.

It performs functions such as:

  • Making laws.
  • Controlling the State Executive.
  • Approving taxation and expenditure.
  • Debating public issues.
  • Representing public opinion.
  • Holding the Council of Ministers accountable.
  • It functions within the constitutional framework of federalism and parliamentary government.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Legislature → Law-Making Body of State

2. Constitutional Framework

The State Legislature is dealt with in:

  • Part VI.
  • Chapter III.
  • Articles 168–212.
  • Article 213 relating to Governor's Ordinance power is closely connected with the legislative framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Legislature → Part VI → Chapter III → Articles 168–212

3. Article 168

Under Article 168, State Legislature consists of:

  • Governor.
  • Legislative Assembly.
  • Legislative Council, where such a Council exists.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 168 → Governor + Assembly + Council where it exists

4. Unicameral Legislature

A unicameral State Legislature consists of:

  • Governor.
  • Legislative Assembly.
  • Most States follow unicameralism.

It avoids:

  • Duplication.
  • Higher administrative cost.
  • Additional delay in law-making.

5. Bicameral Legislature

A bicameral State Legislature consists of:

  • Governor.
  • Legislative Assembly.
  • Legislative Council.
  • The Legislative Council acts mainly as a revising and deliberative chamber.

6. States with Legislative Councils

According to the attached notes, Legislative Councils exist in:

  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Bihar.
  • Karnataka.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Telangana.
  • Uttar Pradesh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Legislative Council States in Source → 6

7. Article 169

Article 169 deals with:

  • Creation of Legislative Council.
  • Abolition of Legislative Council.
  • Parliament may create or abolish a Council only after the concerned Legislative Assembly passes the required resolution.

8. State Assembly Resolution under Article 169

The resolution requires:

  • Majority of total membership of Assembly.
  • Majority of not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 169 State Resolution → Total Membership Majority + 2/3 Present & Voting

9. Parliament's Role under Article 169

After State Assembly passes the required resolution:

  • Parliament may enact the law by simple majority.
  • Such a law is not treated as a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Create/Abolish Legislative Council → State Special Resolution + Parliament Simple Majority

10. Legislative Assembly

Legislative Assembly is also called:

  • Vidhan Sabha.

It is:

  • Lower House.
  • Popular House.
  • Directly elected House.
  • It is the more powerful House in a bicameral State Legislature.

11. Legislative Council

Legislative Council is also called:

  • Vidhan Parishad.

It is:

  • Upper House.
  • Permanent House.
  • Mostly indirectly elected.
  • It cannot be dissolved.

12. Governor as Part of Legislature

  • Governor is an integral part of State Legislature.
  • Governor is not a Member of either House.

Legislative functions include:

  • Summoning.
  • Proroguing.
  • Dissolving Assembly.
  • Addressing Legislature.
  • Assenting to Bills.
  • Ordinance-making when Legislature is not in session.

13. Parliamentary Government at State Level

  • Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to Legislative Assembly.
  • Executive is closely linked with Legislature.

Legislature controls Government through:

  • Questions.
  • Motions.
  • Budget.
  • Committees.
  • No-Confidence Motion.

14. Legislative Competence

State Legislature primarily legislates on:

  • State List.
  • Concurrent List.

Examples of State List subjects given in the source include:

  • Police.
  • Public Order.
  • Agriculture.
  • Public Health.
  • Local Government.
  • Land.

15. Concurrent List Subjects

Examples mentioned in the attachment include:

  • Education.
  • Forests.
  • Marriage.
  • Criminal Law.
  • Electricity.
  • Labour Welfare.
  • Both Parliament and State Legislature may legislate on Concurrent List matters.

16. Financial Powers

State Legislature:

  • Approves State Budget.
  • Votes on Demands for Grants.
  • Passes Appropriation Bills.
  • Authorises taxation.
  • Exercises financial control.
  • Legislative Assembly has greater financial authority than Legislative Council.

17. Executive Control

The Legislature controls Executive through:

  • Question Hour.
  • Zero Hour.
  • Calling Attention.
  • Adjournment Motion.
  • No-Confidence Motion.
  • Budget discussions.
  • Legislative Committees.

18. Legislative Assembly — Article 170

  • Article 170 deals with composition of Legislative Assemblies.

Members are:

  • Directly elected.
  • Elected from territorial constituencies.
  • Chosen through universal adult suffrage.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 170 → Legislative Assembly Composition

19. Assembly Strength

The source states:

  • Maximum strength → 500.
  • Minimum strength → 60.
  • Parliament may provide smaller Assemblies for certain States.
📌 Must-Memorise

Assembly Strength → Normally 60–500

20. States with Fewer than 60 Members

Examples mentioned in the source:

  • Goa.
  • Sikkim.
  • Mizoram.
  • Arunachal Pradesh.

21. Assembly Election Method

Members are elected through:

  • Direct Election.
  • Universal Adult Suffrage.
  • Secret Ballot.
  • First-Past-the-Post system.
📌 Must-Memorise

Assembly Election → Direct + FPTP

22. Article 173 — Assembly Qualifications

A candidate must:

  • Be a citizen of India.
  • Have completed 25 years for Legislative Assembly.
  • Possess qualifications prescribed by Parliament.
  • Not suffer disqualification.
📌 Must-Memorise

MLA Minimum Age → 25 Years

23. Article 188 — Oath

Every elected Member must take:

  • Oath.
  • Or affirmation

before taking the seat.

  • Oath is administered by a person authorised by Governor.

24. Article 172 — Assembly Term

Normal term of Legislative Assembly:

  • Five years from first meeting.
  • Assembly may be dissolved earlier.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 172 → Assembly Term → 5 Years

25. Extension during National Emergency

During Article 352 Emergency:

Parliament may extend Assembly term:

  • One year at a time.

Extension cannot continue beyond:

  • Six months after Emergency ends.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Emergency Extension → 1 Year at a Time

After Emergency → Maximum 6 Months

26. Article 174 — Sessions

Governor:

  • Summons Assembly.
  • Prorogues Legislature.
  • Dissolves Assembly.

Gap between two sessions cannot exceed:

  • Six months.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 174 → Sessions + Prorogation + Dissolution

27. Article 189 — Quorum

Quorum is:

  • Ten Members, or
  • One-tenth of total membership,
  • Whichever is greater.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Legislature Quorum → 10 or 1/10, Whichever Greater

28. Assembly Presiding Officers

Legislative Assembly elects:

  • Speaker.
  • Deputy Speaker.

29. Assembly Legislative Powers

Assembly:

  • Passes Ordinary Bills.
  • Enacts State laws.
  • Amends State laws.
  • Repeals laws.

Legislates on:

  • State List.
  • Concurrent List.

30. Assembly Financial Supremacy

Legislative Assembly:

  • Passes Money Bills.
  • Votes on Demands for Grants.
  • Passes Appropriation Bills.
  • Exercises primary control over State finances.

31. Assembly and Council of Ministers

Council of Ministers is collectively responsible:

  • Only to Legislative Assembly.

Assembly can remove Government through:

  • No-Confidence Motion.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Government Confidence → Legislative Assembly Only

32. Electoral Functions of MLAs

Elected MLAs participate in election of:

  • President of India.
  • Rajya Sabha Members.

33. Constitutional Functions of Assembly

Assembly may:

  • Ratify specified Constitutional Amendments where required.
  • Discuss reports.
  • Debate State policy.
  • Participate in constitutional processes.

34. Vacancies in Assembly

A seat may become vacant due to:

  • Resignation.
  • Death.
  • Disqualification.
  • Unauthorised absence.
  • Election being declared void.

35. Article 191 — Disqualification

Disqualification grounds include:

  • Office of Profit.
  • Unsound mind.
  • Undischarged insolvency.
  • Loss of citizenship.
  • Disqualification under parliamentary law.
  • Defection under Tenth Schedule.

36. Legislative Council — Article 171

Article 171 deals with:

  • Composition of Legislative Council.

Council is:

  • Permanent.
  • Mostly indirectly elected.
  • Revising chamber.

37. Council Strength

Total Council strength shall not exceed:

  • One-third of Assembly strength.

It shall generally not be less than:

  • 40 members.
  • Parliament may provide exceptions by law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Legislative Council → ≤ 1/3 Assembly Strength → Normally ≥ 40

38. One-Third Local Bodies

Approximately one-third of Legislative Council members are elected by:

  • Municipalities.
  • District Panchayats.
  • Other prescribed Local Authorities.

39. One-Twelfth Graduates

Approximately one-twelfth are elected by:

  • Graduates.
  • Of at least three years' standing.
  • Residing in State.

40. One-Twelfth Teachers

Approximately one-twelfth are elected by:

  • Teachers.
  • With at least three years' experience.
  • In institutions not lower than secondary school level.

41. One-Third by MLAs

Approximately one-third are elected by:

  • Members of Legislative Assembly.
  • From persons who are not Assembly members.

42. Governor-Nominated Members

Remaining members are nominated by Governor from persons with special knowledge or practical experience in:

  • Literature.
  • Science.
  • Art.
  • Cooperative Movement.
  • Social Service.
📌 Must-Memorise

Council Nomination Fields → Literature + Science + Art + Cooperative Movement + Social Service

43. Council Election Method

Elected members are chosen through:

  • Proportional Representation.
  • Single Transferable Vote.

44. Council Qualifications

A candidate must:

  • Be Indian citizen.
  • Have completed 30 years.
  • Possess qualifications prescribed by Parliament.
  • Not incur disqualification.
📌 Must-Memorise

MLC Minimum Age → 30 Years

45. Council Term

  • Legislative Council is permanent.

Each member serves:

  • Six years.

One-third retire:

  • Every two years.
📌 Must-Memorise

MLC → 6 Years

1/3 Retire → Every 2 Years

46. Council Presiding Officers

Legislative Council elects:

  • Chairman.
  • Deputy Chairman.

47. Council Legislative Role

Legislative Council may:

  • Discuss Bills.
  • Suggest amendments.
  • Review legislation.
  • Delay Ordinary Bills.
  • Function as revising chamber.
  • It cannot permanently block the Assembly.

48. Council and Money Bills

Legislative Council:

  • Cannot introduce Money Bill.
  • Cannot reject it permanently.
  • Cannot amend it.
  • May recommend changes.

Must return it within:

  • 14 days.

49. Council and Executive Responsibility

Council may:

  • Ask questions.
  • Debate policy.
  • Discuss public issues.
  • Council of Ministers is not collectively responsible to Council.
  • Council cannot remove Government through No-Confidence Motion.

50. Delay of Ordinary Bills by Council

  • Council may reject or delay an Ordinary Bill.
  • Assembly may pass it again.
  • Assembly ultimately prevails.
  • Council functions as a delaying chamber, not a veto chamber.

51. Legislative Council vs Rajya Sabha

Rajya Sabha:

  • Upper House of Parliament.
  • Permanent.
  • Represents States in Union Legislature.
  • Cannot be abolished as a House of Parliament.

Legislative Council:

  • Upper House of State Legislature.
  • Permanent.
  • Exists only in some States.
  • Can be created or abolished under Article 169.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Rajya Sabha ≠ State Legislative Council in Constitutional Status

52. Article 178 — Speaker and Deputy Speaker

Legislative Assembly elects:

  • Speaker.
  • Deputy Speaker.
  • Both are chosen from among Assembly members.

53. Speaker's Role

Speaker is:

  • Presiding Officer.
  • Guardian of Assembly.

Authority maintaining:

  • Order.
  • Dignity.
  • Parliamentary procedure.
  • Discipline.

54. Speaker's Continuance after Dissolution

  • Speaker continues in office even after Assembly dissolution.
  • Continues until immediately before first meeting of new Assembly.
  • This provides institutional continuity.

55. Speaker's Resignation

Speaker resigns to:

  • Deputy Speaker.

Deputy Speaker resigns to:

  • Speaker.
📌 Must-Memorise

Speaker → Resigns to Deputy Speaker

56. Speaker's Removal

Removal requires:

  • Resolution of Legislative Assembly.
  • Majority of all the then members.

At least:

  • 14 days' notice.
📌 Must-Memorise

Speaker Removal → Effective Majority + 14 Days

57. Article 181

  • Speaker cannot preside when resolution for own removal is under consideration.
  • Similar rule applies to Deputy Speaker.

58. Speaker's Main Functions

Speaker:

  • Presides over House.
  • Maintains discipline.
  • Interprets Rules.
  • Decides points of order.
  • Certifies Money Bills.
  • Exercises casting vote.
  • Protects privileges.
  • Controls Assembly Secretariat.
  • Performs committee functions.
  • Decides defection cases.

59. Speaker and Money Bill

  • Speaker decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill in the State Legislature.
  • Certification carries major constitutional significance.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Money Bill Certification → Assembly Speaker

60. Speaker's Casting Vote

  • Speaker ordinarily does not vote.

In case of equality:

  • Speaker exercises casting vote.

61. Speaker and Anti-Defection

Under Tenth Schedule:

  • Speaker decides defection questions concerning MLAs.

Decision is subject to:

  • Judicial Review.

62. Deputy Speaker

Deputy Speaker:

  • Presides when Speaker is absent.
  • Exercises Speaker's powers while presiding.
  • Performs constitutional and procedural duties assigned.

63. Article 182 — Council Chairman

Legislative Council elects:

  • Chairman.
  • Deputy Chairman

from among its members.

64. Chairman's Term

Chairman remains in office until:

  • Resignation.
  • Removal.
  • Ceasing to be Council member.
  • Council being permanent means no dissolution-related interruption.

65. Chairman's Resignation

Chairman resigns to:

  • Deputy Chairman.

Deputy Chairman resigns to:

  • Chairman.

66. Chairman's Removal

Requires:

  • Resolution of Legislative Council.
  • Majority of all the then members.
  • 14 days' prior notice.

67. Article 185

  • Chairman cannot preside while own removal resolution is considered.
  • Same principle applies to Deputy Chairman.

68. Chairman's Functions

Chairman:

  • Presides.
  • Maintains order.
  • Interprets Rules.
  • Decides points of order.
  • Exercises casting vote.
  • Protects privileges.
  • Performs committee functions.
  • Exercises administrative control over Council Secretariat.

69. Speaker vs Chairman

Speaker:

  • Legislative Assembly.
  • Certifies Money Bills.
  • Assembly may remove Government.
  • Directly elected House.

Chairman:

  • Legislative Council.
  • Does not certify Money Bills.
  • Council cannot remove Government.
  • Upper House.

70. Chairman of Council vs Rajya Sabha Chairman

Legislative Council Chairman:

  • Elected by Council members.
  • Member of Council.
  • State Legislature.

Rajya Sabha Chairman:

  • Vice-President of India ex-officio.
  • Not Rajya Sabha member.
  • Parliament.

71. Article 196 — Introduction and Passing of Bills

  • Article 196 governs introduction and passage of Bills in State Legislature.
  • Ordinary Bills may generally originate in either House in bicameral States.

72. Meaning of a Bill

  • A Bill is a draft proposal for law.

After passage and required assent:

  • It becomes an Act.

73. Types of State Bills

State Legislature may deal with:

  • Ordinary Bills.
  • Money Bills.
  • Financial Bills.
  • Constitutional Amendment Bills are introduced only in Parliament.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Constitutional Amendment Bill → Not Introduced in State Legislature

74. Ordinary Bill

Ordinary Bill deals with matters other than:

  • Money Bills.
  • Financial Bills.

Examples may relate to:

  • Agriculture.
  • Police.
  • Public Health.
  • Local Government.
  • Education.
  • Social welfare.

75. Introduction of Ordinary Bill

An Ordinary Bill may be introduced:

  • In Assembly.
  • In Council where it exists.

It may be introduced by:

  • Minister.
  • Private Member.

76. First Reading

  • Bill is introduced.
  • Title and objectives are presented.
  • Detailed discussion ordinarily does not occur.

77. Second Reading

This is the most detailed stage and may include:

  • General Discussion.
  • Committee Stage.
  • Consideration Stage.

78. Committee Stage

Bill may be referred to:

  • Select Committee.
  • Joint Committee.
  • Department-related Committee.

Committee examines:

  • Clauses.
  • Legal implications.
  • Administrative feasibility.

79. Consideration Stage

House examines:

  • Clause by clause.
  • Proposed amendments.

Members may:

  • Accept.
  • Reject.
  • Modify provisions.

80. Third Reading

  • Final discussion.
  • Bill put to vote.

If passed:

  • Sent to other House where applicable.

81. Article 197 — Council's Power over Ordinary Bills

  • Legislative Council cannot permanently block an Ordinary Bill passed by Assembly.
  • Assembly may pass it again.
  • Assembly ultimately prevails.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 197 → Assembly Primacy over Ordinary Bills

82. No Joint Sitting in State Legislature

There is no constitutional provision for Joint Sitting between:

  • Legislative Assembly.
  • Legislative Council.
  • Deadlock is resolved through Assembly's constitutional supremacy.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

State Legislature → No Joint Sitting

83. Article 200 — Governor's Assent

After passage, Governor may:

  • Give assent.
  • Withhold assent.
  • Return an Ordinary Bill.
  • Reserve Bill for President.

84. Article 201

  • Deals with Bills reserved for President.
  • President may act according to constitutional procedure after reservation.

85. Government Bill

Introduced by:

  • Minister.
  • Reflects Government policy.
  • Generally has greater likelihood of passage due to Government majority support.

86. Private Member's Bill

Introduced by:

  • Member who is not a Minister.
  • Reflects individual legislative initiative.
  • Comparatively few become law.

87. Lapsing of Bills

On Assembly dissolution:

  • Bill pending in Assembly → Lapses.
  • Bill passed by Assembly but pending Governor's assent → Does not lapse.
  • Bill pending only in Council and not yet passed by Assembly → Does not lapse.
  • Bill passed by Assembly but pending in Council → Generally lapses.

88. Article 199 — Money Bill

  • Article 199 defines Money Bill at State level.
  • A Money Bill contains only specified financial matters.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 199 → State Money Bill

89. Matters in State Money Bill

May include:

  • Taxation.
  • State borrowing.
  • Consolidated Fund.
  • Contingency Fund.
  • Appropriation.
  • Charged expenditure.
  • State accounts.
  • Incidental matters.

90. Tax Matters

Money Bill may deal with:

  • Imposition of tax.
  • Abolition.
  • Remission.
  • Alteration.
  • Regulation.

91. Borrowing and Funds

Money Bill may deal with:

  • State borrowing.
  • Consolidated Fund.
  • Contingency Fund.
  • Withdrawal of money.
  • Appropriation.

92. Introduction of Money Bill

Money Bill:

  • Only in Legislative Assembly.
  • Cannot originate in Council.

Requires:

  • Prior recommendation of Governor.

Source states it is introduced by:

  • Minister.
📌 Must-Memorise

Money Bill → Assembly Only + Governor's Prior Recommendation

93. Role of Speaker in Money Bill

  • Speaker certifies whether Bill is a Money Bill.
  • This certification is constitutionally significant.

94. Council's Role in Money Bill

Council:

  • Cannot reject.
  • Cannot amend.
  • May recommend changes.

Must return Bill within:

  • 14 days.

95. If Council Does Not Return in 14 Days

Bill is deemed passed by both Houses:

  • In form passed by Assembly.

96. Assembly and Council Recommendations

Assembly may:

  • Accept all recommendations.
  • Accept some.
  • Reject all.
  • Assembly's decision is final.

97. Governor and Money Bill

After passage, Governor may:

  • Give assent.
  • Reserve Bill for President where constitutionally required.
  • Money Bill cannot be returned for reconsideration in the manner applicable to Ordinary Bills.

98. Article 207 — Financial Bills

  • Financial Bills are governed by Article 207.

They may combine:

  • Financial provisions.
  • Other provisions.

Therefore:

  • Financial Bill is not necessarily a Money Bill.

99. Article 202 — State Budget

Constitutional term:

  • Annual Financial Statement.

Common term:

  • State Budget.

Contains:

  • Estimated receipts.
  • Estimated expenditure.
  • Revenue proposals.
  • Fiscal policy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 202 → State Budget / Annual Financial Statement

100. Article 203 — Demands for Grants

Legislative Assembly:

  • Discusses.
  • Approves.
  • Rejects.
  • Reduces Demands for Grants.

Legislative Council:

  • May discuss.
  • Cannot vote.
📌 Must-Memorise

Demands for Grants → Assembly Votes

101. Article 204 — Appropriation Bill

  • Introduced after Demands for Grants.

Authorises withdrawal from:

  • Consolidated Fund of State.
  • Public money requiring appropriation cannot be withdrawn without legal authorisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 204 → State Appropriation Bill

102. Article 205

Article 205 deals with:

  • Supplementary Grants.
  • Additional Grants.
  • Excess Grants.

103. Supplementary Grant

  • Used where original Budget allocation becomes insufficient.

104. Additional Grant

  • Used for a new service not included in original Budget.

105. Excess Grant

  • Used when actual expenditure exceeds amount sanctioned.
  • Requires subsequent legislative approval.

106. Article 206 — Vote on Account

  • Temporary financial authority when full Budget is not yet passed.
  • Allows routine expenditure for short period.

107. Vote of Credit

Used when:

  • Exact expenditure cannot be estimated.
  • Extraordinary situation exists.

Source gives examples such as:

  • War.
  • Emergency.

108. Exceptional Grant

  • Used for special purpose outside ordinary annual service of Government.

109. Charged Expenditure

Charged expenditure:

  • May be discussed.
  • Is not voted.

Examples in source include:

  • Governor's salary and allowances.
  • High Court Judges' salaries and allowances.
  • Interest on State debt.
  • Other constitutionally charged expenditure.

110. Legislative Committees

  • Committees are constituted under Rules of Procedure.
  • Article 208 provides constitutional basis for House rules.

Committees are often described as:

  • Mini Legislature.
  • Working engines of Legislature.

111. Purpose of Committees

Committees help:

  • Examine Bills in detail.
  • Scrutinise expenditure.
  • Study administration.
  • Investigate issues.
  • Seek expert opinion.
  • Improve accountability.

112. Main Committee Types

Broadly include:

  • Financial Committees.
  • Department-related Committees.
  • House Committees.
  • Inquiry and Advisory Committees.

113. Public Accounts Committee

PAC examines:

  • CAG reports.
  • Government expenditure.
  • Appropriation Accounts.
  • Whether money was spent according to legislative approval.

114. PAC Chairperson

In many Legislatures, by convention:

  • Chairperson is chosen from Opposition.
  • This supports impartial financial scrutiny.

115. Estimates Committee

Examines:

  • Budget estimates.
  • Economy in expenditure.
  • Administrative efficiency.
  • Organisational improvement.
  • Future expenditure planning.

116. Committee on Public Undertakings

COPU examines:

  • State PSUs.
  • Government corporations.
  • Financial performance.
  • Administrative efficiency.
  • CAG reports concerning public undertakings.

117. PAC vs Estimates Committee

PAC:

  • Examines expenditure already incurred.
  • Relies heavily on CAG Reports.

Estimates Committee:

  • Examines proposed expenditure.
  • Focuses on economy and efficiency.

118. Committee on Privileges

Examines:

  • Breach of privilege.
  • Complaints affecting Legislature's dignity.
  • Rights and privileges of members.

119. Committee on Petitions

Examines petitions from:

  • Citizens.
  • Organisations.
  • Interested persons.
  • Reports recommendations to Legislature.

120. Committee on Government Assurances

  • Examines promises, assurances and undertakings made by Ministers in House.
  • Checks whether they have been fulfilled.

121. Business Advisory Committee

  • Plans legislative agenda.
  • Allocates time.
  • Recommends order of business.

122. Rules Committee

  • Reviews Rules of Procedure.
  • Examines parliamentary practice.
  • Recommends procedural reforms.

123. Ethics Committee

  • Examines ethical conduct.
  • Considers misconduct.
  • Promotes legislative standards.

124. Committee on Subordinate Legislation

Examines:

  • Rules.
  • Regulations.
  • Bye-laws.
  • Notifications.
  • Orders.

Purpose:

  • Ensure delegated legislation remains within parent Act.

125. Committee on Papers Laid on the Table

Examines whether required:

  • Reports.
  • Notifications.
  • Rules.
  • Statutory documents

have been properly laid before Legislature.

126. Article 187

Article 187 provides for:

  • Secretariat of State Legislature.
  • Independent legislative secretariat supports institutional autonomy.

127. Article 190

Deals with:

  • Vacation of seats.
  • Resignation.
  • Double membership.
  • Absence.

128. Article 192

  • Governor decides questions of disqualification of State legislators.

Governor must obtain opinion of:

  • Election Commission of India.
  • Decision is made in accordance with that constitutional process.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 192 → Governor + Election Commission Opinion

129. Article 193

  • Provides penalty for sitting or voting when not qualified or entitled.

130. Article 208

  • Each House may make Rules regulating its procedure and conduct of business.

131. Article 209

  • Parliament/State constitutional framework permits regulation by law of legislative procedure relating to financial business.

132. Article 210

Language of State Legislature may include:

  • State Official Language or Languages.
  • Hindi.
  • English

subject to constitutional provisions and applicable law.

133. Article 211

  • Conduct of Supreme Court and High Court Judges cannot ordinarily be discussed in State Legislature.
  • Constitutional exceptions operate where applicable.

134. Article 212

  • Courts shall not inquire into State legislative proceedings merely on ground of procedural irregularity.
  • Constitutional violations may remain subject to judicial scrutiny under broader constitutional doctrine.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 212 → Courts and State Legislative Proceedings

135. Article 213

  • Governor may promulgate Ordinance when Legislature is not in session.
  • Closely connected with State legislative functioning.

136. Anglo-Indian Nomination — Historical Position

  • Article 333 earlier allowed Governor to nominate an Anglo-Indian member to Assembly where representation was considered inadequate.

The attached notes state this provision was discontinued through:

  • 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020.

137. Seventh Constitutional Amendment, 1956

The attachment links it with:

  • States Reorganisation.
  • Restructuring legislative representation.
  • Changes in Assemblies and Councils.
  • One Governor for two or more States.

138. Forty-Second Amendment, 1976

Important State-legislative effects in source include shifting subjects from State List to Concurrent List such as:

  • Education.
  • Forests.
  • Protection of Wild Animals and Birds.
  • Weights and Measures.
📌 Must-Memorise

42nd Amendment → Important State-to-Concurrent List Transfers

139. Forty-Fourth Amendment, 1978

Restored normal Assembly term:

  • From Emergency-era six years.
  • Back to five years.
  • Reinforced democratic safeguards.

140. Fifty-Second Amendment, 1985

Introduced:

  • Anti-Defection Law.
  • Tenth Schedule.

Applied to:

  • MLAs.
  • MLCs.

141. Sixty-First Amendment, 1988

Reduced voting age:

  • 21 → 18.
  • Article 326.
  • Expanded electorate for Assembly elections.
📌 Must-Memorise

142. Seventy-Third Amendment, 1992

  • Constitutionalised Panchayati Raj.
  • Required States to enact local-government laws.
  • Increased State Legislature's role in decentralisation.

143. Seventy-Fourth Amendment, 1992

  • Constitutionalised Municipalities.
  • Expanded State Legislature's urban-governance responsibilities.

144. Eighty-Fourth Amendment, 2001

  • Continued freeze on readjustment of Assembly seats based on population.
  • Allowed limited delimitation within constitutional framework.

145. Eighty-Seventh Amendment, 2003

Allowed delimitation using:

  • 2001 Census figures.
  • Total seat-allocation freeze continued under constitutional framework stated in source.

146. Ninety-First Amendment, 2003

Important effects:

  • Strengthened Anti-Defection Law.
  • Removed one-third split protection.
  • Retained two-thirds merger.

Limited State Ministry size to:

  • 15% of Assembly strength.
  • Restricted defectors from ministerial office until constitutionally eligible.

147. Ninety-Seventh Amendment, 2011

  • Granted constitutional recognition to Cooperative Societies.
  • State laws concerning cooperatives were required to operate within constitutional framework, subject to later judicial developments.

148. One Hundred and First Amendment, 2016

  • Introduced GST.
  • Required changes in State taxation laws.
  • Strengthened Union–State financial coordination.

149. One Hundred and Second Amendment, 2018

Granted constitutional status to:

  • National Commission for Backward Classes.
  • State Legislature continued exercising powers within constitutional competence on backward-class matters.

150. One Hundred and Fourth Amendment, 2020

Source highlights:

  • Anglo-Indian nomination to State Assemblies discontinued.
  • SC/ST legislative reservation extended.

151. One Hundred and Fifth Amendment, 2021

Restored States' power to identify and maintain:

  • State List of Socially and Educationally Backward Classes.
  • Strengthened State role in reservation policy.
📌 Must-Memorise

105th Amendment → States' SEBC Identification Power

152. Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu, 1992

Supreme Court held:

  • Tenth Schedule constitutionally valid.
  • Speaker acts as constitutional authority.
  • Speaker's defection decisions are subject to Judicial Review.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kihoto Hollohan → Anti-Defection + Judicial Review

153. S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, 1994

Supreme Court held:

  • Majority should ordinarily be tested on Assembly floor.
  • Governor's Article 356 report is reviewable.
  • Article 356 cannot be arbitrarily used.

154. Jagdambika Pal Case, 1998

Supreme Court directed:

  • Immediate Floor Test.
  • Majority disputes should be resolved in House.

155. Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India, 2006

  • Premature dissolution of Bihar Assembly was held unconstitutional.
  • Political assumptions cannot substitute constitutional legislative process.

156. B.P. Singhal v. Union of India, 2010

  • Governor holds office during President's pleasure.
  • Removal cannot be arbitrary or politically capricious.
  • Decision indirectly protects institutional functioning of State Legislature.

157. Mohd. Saeed Siddiqui v. State of Uttar Pradesh, 2014

  • Speaker's Money Bill certification carries constitutional significance.
  • Courts generally exercise restraint according to the source.

158. Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker, 2016

Source states:

  • Speaker should not decide disqualification petitions while valid removal notice against Speaker is pending.
  • Governor cannot interfere beyond constitutional limits in legislative functioning.

159. K.S. Puttaswamy Aadhaar Case, 2018

  • Majority upheld Aadhaar Act as Money Bill.
  • Dissent questioned classification.
  • Though parliamentary, case influenced constitutional debate regarding Money Bill scope relevant to Article 199 parallels.

160. Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank, 2019

  • Important questions concerning scope of Money Bills were referred to larger Bench.
  • Principles are relevant to analogous State Money Bill issues.

161. Keisham Meghachandra Singh, 2020

Supreme Court observed defection petitions should ordinarily be decided within:

  • Three months.
📌 Must-Memorise

Keisham Meghachandra → 2020 → Defection Petitions Normally 3 Months

162. Searchlight Case, 1959

Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha:

  • Legislative privileges receive constitutional protection.
  • Courts ordinarily respect legislative autonomy within constitutional limits.

163. Keshav Singh Case, 1964

  • Legislative privileges are important.
  • They remain subject to Constitution.
  • Judicial Review is available in appropriate cases.

Can Legislative Council remove Government through No-Confidence Motion? → No.

To whom does Speaker resign? → Deputy Speaker.

What majority removes Speaker? → Majority of all the then members.

What notice is required? → 14 days.

Can Speaker preside during own removal motion? → No.

Which Article restricts Council's power over Ordinary Bills? → Article 197.

Can Legislative Council permanently block an Ordinary Bill? → No.

Is there a Joint Sitting of State Assembly and Council? → No.

Which House ultimately prevails? → Legislative Assembly.

Where can Money Bill originate? → Legislative Assembly only.

Whose prior recommendation is required? → Governor.

Can Private Member introduce a Money Bill under the source framework? → No.

Can Council reject a Money Bill? → No.

Can Council amend it? → No; it may recommend.

What if Council fails to return in 14 days? → Bill is deemed passed in Assembly form.

Can Governor return a Money Bill for reconsideration? → No.

Which Article deals with reserved Bills? → Article 201.
